https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/09/gajd.text: Menü Kereső Janza Benedek, Gajdos László minisztériumának főosztályvezetője halt meg a Bécsi úton történt balesetben Belföld Mizsur András Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Balesetben meghalt Janza Benedek, az Élő Környezetért Felelős Minisztérium egyik főosztályvezetője. Gajdos László élő környezetért felelős miniszter Facebook-oldalán fejezte ki részvétét a családnak. „Benedek halála mindannyiunk számára felfoghatatlan veszteség. Kiváló szakember volt, aki a mindennapokban példás elhivatottsággal, magas szintű tudással és fáradhatatlan munkabírással vezette a főosztályt. Egy fiatal, életerős, mindig segítőkész kollégát és egy gondoskodó édesapát veszítettünk el, akinek emléke és munkája kitörölhetetlen nyomot hagy a Minisztérium közösségében” – írta. A minisztérium saját halottjának tekinti a főosztályvezetőt. Gajdos a posztja alatt megosztott egy szerdai hírt, ami arról szólt, hogy frontális balesetben meghalt egy biciklis a III. kerületben . Ezek szerint a kerékpáros Janza Benedek volt. A rendőrségi közlemény szerint egy autós a Bécsi úton haladt az Árpád híd irányába, amikor elvesztette uralmát a jármű felett, áttért a szemközti sávba, és frontálisan ütközött egy szembejövő kerékpárossal, majd egy autóbusszal. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Shabana Mahmood: ‘My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.’ Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Shabana Mahmood: ‘My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.’ Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty Images Immigration and asylum UK threatens to ban Eritreans over returns policy Move comes after east African country abruptly withdrew returns cooperation earlier this year UK politics live – latest updates Rajeev Syal and Diane Taylor Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.45 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Eritreans could be stopped from coming to the UK unless the country agrees to accept more rejected asylum seekers and criminals, Shabana Mahmood has warned. VIPs and officials from the east African country have already been stripped of fast-track access to UK visas after their government refused to cooperate with the return of its nationals, the home secretary said. The warning comes after Eritrea abruptly withdrew returns cooperation earlier this year, the Home Office said. Refugee organisations have warned that the UK should not get drawn into rejecting applicants for asylum from Eritrea because it is a war-torn country and the UK usually accepts the vast majority of applicants, who are often escaping famine and conflict. Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals. Mahmood said: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused. “My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK. “I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.” The move follows similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025. Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February. In March, ministers also placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the home secretary accused them of exploiting Britain’s generosity to claim asylum. Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were also halted, as were work visas for Afghans. Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality. After the success of the previous sanction threats, Mahmood warned other countries that they faced similar visa restrictions if they continued to refuse to take back their criminals, illegal migrants and rejected asylum seekers. India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Somalia, Egypt and Gabon have been identified as resistant to taking back illegal migrants and could face sanctions. Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said roughly 7,000 applications for asylum came from Eritreans, about 8% of the total. About 84% are successful on first application and more will be successful on appeal, she said. “There are different types of threats that can be made such as stopping student visas, or stopping visit visas. It will be interesting to see what kind of impact this has on the number of returns.” Reacting to Mahmood’s announcement, one Eritrean asylum seeker said any returnees would “be put in prison and may never be able to get out”. UN experts say that the human rights situation in Eritrea continues to be dire. Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, the special rapporteur on human rights in Eritrea, said there were no signs of meaningful improvement in the country’s human rights situation. “There remain reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity continue in Eritrea,” he said when launching a report this year into the human rights situation. “Regrettably, the core human rights issues that prompted the creation of this mandate 14 years ago remain mostly unresolved. “The ongoing systematic, and widespread enforced disappearance and prolonged incommunicado detention without charge or trial, torture, and the persecution of political opponents, journalists, and members of religious communities remain central features of governance in Eritrea.” Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International’s policy lead on refugee and migrant rights said: “As Amnesty and others have documented, Eritrea has an appalling human rights record – including arbitrarily detaining people forced to return and indefinite and forced conscription in circumstances that in some cases amount to slavery. “It has not become any less safe following the election in this country of a Labour government in 2024 or Shabana Mahmood beginning her term at the Home Office in 2025.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Eritrea Shabana Mahmood Migration Refugees Home Office news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: Matilda Davis was ‘physically and emotionally exhausted’ when she took her own life, said Manuela Perteghella, the MP for Stratford-upon-Avon. Composite: Guardian View image in fullscreen Matilda Davis was ‘physically and emotionally exhausted’ when she took her own life, said Manuela Perteghella, the MP for Stratford-upon-Avon. Composite: Guardian Mental health Burnham backs mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after parent-carer Matilda Davis’s death Former art teacher, who cared for her disabled son, ‘received almost no support’, said her local MP Manuela Perteghella Josh Halliday North of England editor Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.46 EDT First published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham has backed mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after the “devastating” death of Matilda Davis, a parent-carer who killed herself minutes after meeting professionals. The Guardian revealed in August how the “absolutely inspirational” 36-year-old had taken her life after feeling “completely exhausted” and failed by England’s social care system. Davis, a former art teacher, had told multiple professionals she was struggling to cope with the significant care for her seven-year-old son and “paralysed with anxiety” about her looming divorce from her estranged husband. She died on 3 October last year, minutes after an emotional meeting with social workers who had not received suicide prevention training. Burnham was asked about Davis’s case at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday and said he supported the extension of this training to all local authorities in England. Manuela Perteghella, the Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-upon-Avon, where Davis lived, said: “My constituent Matilda Davis was a wonderful and devoted mum and a full-time carer for her disabled seven-year-old child. Despite providing round the clock care, she received almost no support leaving her physically and emotionally exhausted. “Last October, social workers visited Matilda and she took her own life 15 minutes after they left. She was 36.” Perteghella highlighted University of Birmingham research showing that 41% of parent-carers have contemplated suicide, and asked Burnham to meet her and Matilda’s family to discuss “mandatory suicide prevention training for local authorities and other measures so that no more normal families suffer such a devastating loss”. Burnham replied: “I will ensure that a minister meets the honourable lady to discuss that proposal because I find myself in agreement with it.” The prime minister praised the Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, for his work campaigning on behalf of unpaid carers, whose failure by the state has been brought into light by an award-winning Guardian investigation into the carer’s allowance scandal . Burnham said these carers, who often gave up work and other commitments while saving the government billions of pounds to look after severely disabled loved ones, could often “sink under their responsibilities and find it very, very difficult”. He added: “Sadly in the case of Matilda, [Perteghella’s] constituent, obviously a devastating situation. I will arrange that meeting and I thank [Perteghella] for raising it in the House [of Commons] today.” View image in fullscreen Manuela Perteghella, the Lib Dem MP for Stratford-upon Avon, asked Andy Burnham to meet her and Davis’s family to discuss the mandatory training. Photograph: House of Commons/PA At Davis’s inquest in March, social workers admitted they did not ask her whether she had thoughts of suicide despite knowing she was in significant distress, nor was she directed to crisis organisations. As a result, the coroner, Deborah Sewell, issued a rare prevention of future deaths notice ordering Warwickshire council to make suicide prevention training mandatory for 600 members of staff, primarily social workers. Davis’s brother, Joel Harley-Davis, said the family was “really reassured” by Burnham’s response and that his sister would have been “proud” to make a positive difference. “We all believe that this training would have been enough to save Matilda’s life,” he said. “If those social workers had asked her [whether she was considering ending her life] Matilda was so honest she would have said yes. “This needs to be made mandatory – you can’t leave it up to councils to decide whether to put it in place because it creates a postcode lottery. It doesn’t need to be this really expensive thing. All the literature and advice says that if in doubt about whether someone is suicidal, ask that direct difficult question.” Guidance issued by the mental health charity Mind states that it is best practice not to “skirt around the topic of suicide” and instead ask direct questions such as: “Are you having suicidal thoughts?” when speaking to someone who might want to kill themselves. Harley-Davis, 30, said his sister felt “failed and let down” by England’s social care system and was passionate about advocating on behalf of other parent-carers. He added: “Matilda was an incredibly stoic individual but that’s not to say she didn’t need someone to offer that respite. “Matilda needed that professional support and a degree of empathy and I don’t think she got that, especially on the day she died.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org , or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counsellor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14.
